query: The Masked Night {Tonight every guest wears a mask, and nobody says why. The landlady hands you one too, plain black, no feathers.|The masks again. One guest, in lacquered silver, asks for you by the colour of your mask.|The masked night. The silver mask is here, and has saved you the seat beside it.} Without faces the room is easier to read, and harder. Sit with the masks {You learn to read a room by its hands. You go home with heavy pockets, no names, and a feeling you can't put down.|The silver mask asks you nothing at all, and tips like a duke. You lie awake wondering who that was.|Behind the masks the guests say what they mean. You come home rich and a little colder.} {A masked guest won't take no for an answer, and nobody can see who it is. You leave by the back stair with a few coins and a very bad feeling.|The silver mask leans too close, and nobody else in the room seems to notice. You go home by the long way.|A guest takes your mask off, laughing, in front of everyone. Someone at the far table looks very like a prefect.} Work the door {You take coats at the door all night. The stairwell is freezing, and every coat smells of a different perfume.|You keep the door, and turn away a guest the landlady points out. The draught gets into your bones.|You work the door and watch the masks arrive one by one. The silver one bows to you, which is worse than being spoken to.}
